questions.question: What is the natural walking model for a system-controlled VR tour intended to achieve?
options: Reducing cybersickness by limiting total VR exposure duration
Providing instantaneous movement between two virtual locations
Choosing a shortest path between points of interest
Providing a realistic walking experience by matching optic flow to the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed
questions.explanation: The natural walking model is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow, that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed.

questions.question: What does the natural walking model itself provide with respect to VR experience optimization?
options: It provides no optimization; it can only enhance presence in the virtual world
It chooses a path that minimizes total navigation time
It increases virtual travel speed to shorten travel time
It limits exposure duration to reduce cybersickness
questions.explanation: The natural walking model does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.

questions.question: What does the VR navigation optimization approach that uses the natural walking model do to address cybersickness?
options: It enhances presence in the virtual world to reduce sickness
It controls the duration of exposure in the virtual world
It increases virtual travel speed arbitrarily to reduce sickness
It uses instantaneous teleportation to reduce sickness
questions.explanation: The optimization approach that uses the natural walking model addresses cybersickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

questions.question: Why can a shorter VR exposure duration help eliminate or minimize the onset of cybersickness?
options: Because the degree of cybersickness symptoms rises proportionally as VR session duration increases
Because shorter sessions reduce the amount of visual speed shown to the user
Because shorter sessions make the optic flow match the perceived walking speed better
Because shorter sessions allow arbitrary virtual travel speeds to be used
questions.explanation: Cybersickness in VR is correlated with exposure duration, and the degree of symptoms rises proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so shorter exposure can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset.

questions.question: Which change to a VR experience is expected to increase the duration of VR exposure?
options: Making the virtual environment larger
Reducing the time spent inspecting objects
Increasing the virtual travel speed
Using teleportation between two points
questions.explanation: Exposure duration depends on the size of the virtual world, and a larger environment requires the user to cover a larger geographical area.

questions.question: What constraint applies to virtual travel speed when a realistic walking experience is intended?
options: It must always be the maximum possible travel speed
It can be set to any speed that minimises exposure duration
It must be controlled by the user at all times
It cannot be modified arbitrarily
questions.explanation: For a realistic walking experience, an arbitrary speed imposed on the user while navigating may not be a good idea.

questions.question: What is a limitation of teleportation-type movement in a virtual world?
options: It is the best movement type when naturalness is required
It always increases the total exposure duration
It is not a natural movement and may be unsuitable when naturalness is required
It requires the user to interact with every object
questions.explanation: Teleportation can reduce exposure duration by providing instantaneous movement, but it is not natural and may not be good when naturalness is required.

questions.question: What can manipulating virtual terrain or POI distances help achieve in a VR tour?
options: Making arbitrary virtual travel speed more natural
Reducing travel time and therefore exposure time
Allowing interaction with every object in the environment
Removing the need for points of interest
questions.explanation: Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a semi-interactive VR tour?
options: Travel is user-controlled, and interaction can happen with any object
Interaction can happen freely with every object before navigation
The system prevents all interaction with virtual objects
Travel is automatic, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at POIs
questions.explanation: A semi-interactive tour has system-controlled automatic travel, with users interacting after navigation with only a limited set of objects at POIs, not other objects.

questions.question: In a semi-interactive virtual tour, what happens when a point of interest has reached its pre-estimated maximum interaction time?
options: The system extends the interaction limit until the POI is fully explored
The system ends the entire tour and returns the user to the starting point
The user may continue interacting until they manually choose to leave
The system automatically forces the user to move to another POI
questions.explanation: In a semi-interactive tour, each POI's interaction time is limited in advance, and when that estimated maximum is reached the system moves the user to another POI.

questions.question: What are the two path-optimization problems for controlling exposure duration in a semi-interactive VR tour?
options: Maximize total navigation and interaction time to experience all POIs, or minimize the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit
Minimize total navigation and interaction time to experience all POIs, or maximize POIs within a fixed time limit
Minimize the interaction time at each POI, or maximize the travel speed within a fixed time limit
Minimize total navigation and interaction time to experience some POIs, or maximize total travel distance within a fixed time limit
questions.explanation: The optimum path can either minimize the total navigation and interaction time needed to experience all POIs, or maximize the number of POIs experienced under a fixed navigation-and-interaction time limit.

questions.question: In a semi-interactive VR tour, what does finding an optimum path optimize when interaction time is limited?
options: The naturalness of the user's travel speed
The duration of exposure
The number of POIs available in the environment
The size of the virtual world
questions.explanation: Finding an optimum path under a limited interaction time is used to optimize the duration of exposure.

questions.question: Why can optimizing exposure duration in a VR tour help address cyber sickness?
options: Because a larger virtual world improves wayfinding and prevents discomfort
Because the number of POIs directly determines the onset of cyber sickness
Because teleportation removes all navigation time and makes movement natural
Because exposure duration and cyber sickness are directly related
questions.explanation: Optimizing exposure duration is expected to affect the prevalence and onset of cyber sickness because exposure duration and cyber sickness are directly related.

questions.question: How is the virtual-world portion of a virtual experience modeled for path planning?
options: As a matched zone where the virtual and real environments align exactly
As a triangular mesh in which every surface is built from triangles
As a panoramic video showing the whole virtual environment
As a weighted graph with POIs as vertices and direct paths as weighted edges
questions.explanation: The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph whose vertices are all points of interest and whose weighted edges represent direct connections between them.

questions.question: Why is the graph that represents a virtual world not required to be complete?
options: Because edge weights for disconnected pairs are set to zero
Because some places in a realistic environment may lack a direct path
Because all POIs are always directly connected in a realistic environment
Because a triangular mesh must contain only directly visible triangles
questions.explanation: The graph need not be complete because realistic environments may not provide a direct path between every pair of places.

questions.question: In the graph model, what weight is assigned to a pair of POIs?
options: Euclidean distance for every pair, connected or not
Travel time if directly connected, otherwise a very large value
Interaction time if directly connected, otherwise zero
Euclidean distance if directly connected, otherwise a very large value
questions.explanation: Directly connected POIs receive an edge weight equal to their Euclidean distance, while non-directly connected pairs are assigned a very large infinity-like value.

questions.question: Why may a single virtual object or structure correspond to more than one graph node?
options: Because it can have multiple material surface properties
Because it can be represented by multiple triangular meshes
Because it can contain multiple points of interest
Because it can occupy several matched zones
questions.explanation: Each point of interest is a node, so one object or structure may become several nodes if it contains several POIs.

questions.question: What is the optimization objective for a tour that covers all POIs?
options: Minimize the interaction time spent at each POI under any speed
Find a path visiting all POIs with the least possible time while maintaining realistic speed
Maximize the number of POIs experienced within a fixed exposure time
Minimize the virtual world's size by removing unused POIs
questions.explanation: The all-POI tour problem seeks a path that covers every POI and finishes in the least possible time, while keeping the user's speed realistic.

questions.question: What is the first stage of the travel-time algorithm?
options: Finding the shortest path between two POIs that are not directly connected
Estimating the interaction time needed at each point of interest
Computing the travel time between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model
Computing the total travel time of a path that visits every point of interest
questions.explanation: The first stage is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

questions.question: In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is:
options: The actual instantaneous realistic walking speed plus the visual gain of 2.1
2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
The actual instantaneous realistic walking speed divided by 2.1
The instantaneous step frequency multiplied by the user's height
questions.explanation: The model defines perceived instantaneous walking speed as the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed.

questions.question: For a small distance element dx, what is the instantaneous time dt in the natural walking-speed model?
options: dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed multiplied by dx
dx divided by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
2.1 times dx divided by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
questions.explanation: Because speed is dx/dt and perceived speed is 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed, dt is dx divided by 2.1 times that speed.

questions.question: After solving the natural walking-speed integral with simplifications, what is the travel-time estimate tau_D for a directly connected vertex pair?
options: D/V_naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum from k=1 to n0 of 1/k^2)
D/V_naught times (3 - (16/pi) * sum from k=1 to n0 of 1/(2k-1)^2)
D/V_naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum from k=1 to n0 of 1/(2k-1)^2)
D/V_naught times (1 - (16/pi^2) * sum from k=1 to n0 of 1/(2k-1)^2)
questions.explanation: The solved travel-time estimate is D/V_naught multiplied by 3 minus (16/pi^2) times the sum from k=1 to n0 of 1/(2k-1)^2.

questions.question: In the natural walking-speed model, V_naught is a constant for which given quantity?
options: The instantaneous step frequency f
The actual instantaneous realistic walking speed V_act
The distance D between directly connected nodes
The user's height h
questions.explanation: V_naught is defined as a constant for a given user height h.

questions.question: For a path P containing n vertices, how is the total travel time for P defined?
options: As the integral of dx/(2.1 V_act) over each consecutive edge
As the maximum Euclidean distance between any consecutive vertices
As the average Euclidean distance between all pairs of vertices
As the sum of the Euclidean edge weights between consecutive vertices
questions.explanation: The total travel time for a path is the sum of the edge weights between consecutive vertices, and each such edge weight is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices.

questions.question: What is the travelling salesman problem asking for in a complete graph?
options: The path that maximizes POI importance within a time threshold
The path of minimum total edge weight that need not visit every node
The shortest path that visits each node at least once and returns to the starting node
The shortest path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node
questions.explanation: TSP is defined as finding the shortest possible path in a complete graph that visits each node exactly once and returns to the start, with shortness measured by total edge weight.

questions.question: What problem can occur in the travel-time minimisation graph because it is not assumed to be complete?
options: It may contain disconnected components that make edge weights undefined
It may require a path that maximizes POI importance within a time threshold
It may have no Hamiltonian path covering all nodes exactly once
It may have no shortest path between every pair of vertices
questions.explanation: Because the graph is not assumed to be complete, it may lack a Hamiltonian path, meaning a path that covers all nodes while visiting each exactly once.

questions.question: When two vertices in the original graph are not directly connected, what weight is assigned to their hypothetical edge?
options: The travel time computed by the natural walking-speed model
The average of all edge weights on paths between them
The length of the shortest path between them in the original graph
The Euclidean distance between the two vertices
questions.explanation: For a pair of vertices that are not directly connected, the hypothetical edge is weighted by the shortest path length between them, which is the sum of the edge weights along that shortest path.

questions.question: What guarantees that a shortest path length can be used for a hypothetical edge between two vertices that are not directly connected?
options: The graph is a scene graph
The graph is connected
The graph is complete
The graph is weighted by a time threshold
questions.explanation: The shortest path lengths needed for hypothetical edges are well-defined because the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is connected.

questions.question: What change is made to an original graph G to form the complete graph G'?
options: Only the directly connected edges are kept, and no hypothetical edges are added.
Directly connected edges are replaced by travel times, and a hypothetical edge is added for each pair of vertices not directly connected.
Every pair of vertices is connected by a hypothetical edge weighted by the travel time between them.
Directly connected edges are kept, and a hypothetical edge weighted by the shortest path length in G is added for each pair of vertices not directly connected.
questions.explanation: The original graph is completed by leaving existing edges unchanged and adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path in G for non-direct pairs.

questions.question: What are the edge weights of the complete graph G'' that is given to the solver?
options: The travel time between each pair of vertices.
The Euclidean distance between each pair of vertices.
The shortest path length between each pair of vertices, without converting it to travel time.
The original edge weights of G, unchanged for all pairs.
questions.explanation: After completion, the Euclidean-distance weights are replaced by travel times, so G'' is time-weighted rather than distance-weighted.

questions.question: How is the complete time-weighted graph G'' solved?
options: By searching for a Hamiltonian path directly in the original graph G.
With a standard travelling salesman problem solver, which returns the optimal time and path for G''.
By selecting the longest path that stays below the cybersickness time threshold.
With a new algorithm designed to minimize cybersickness directly in the original graph G.
questions.explanation: G'' can be solved with a standard TSP solver without needing a new algorithm, producing the optimal time and optimal path for the modified graph.

questions.question: How is the TSP solver's path made valid in the original graph G?
options: Each edge whose endpoints were directly connected in G is replaced by a hypothetical edge.
Each edge whose endpoints were not directly connected in G is replaced by the shortest path between those endpoints in G.
Every hypothetical edge is deleted and the remaining edges are returned as the final path.
Each hypothetical edge is replaced only by the Euclidean distance between its endpoints.
questions.explanation: The solver's path may use hypothetical edges, so the post-processing step expands each such edge into the corresponding shortest path in the original graph.

questions.question: What limitation can remain in a very large terrain or virtual environment?
options: The optimal minimum travel time is guaranteed to stay below the cybersickness time threshold.
The optimal minimum travel time may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold.
The complete graph G'' becomes disconnected because the environment is large.
The standard TSP solver cannot return a path for the complete graph G''.
questions.explanation: Even after finding the minimum-time path, the travel time can be too long in a large environment, so the cybersickness-limit goal may be defeated.

questions.question: What motivates the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach?
options: A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may exceed the cybersickness time threshold
A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may require a new TSP algorithm
A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may be shorter than the cybersickness time threshold
A minimum-time route covering all points of interest may cover too few points of interest
questions.explanation: The all-points minimum-time approach can still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, so a time limit can be used to maximize covered points within that limit.

questions.question: How is the virtual world graph initially represented in the minimum-time approach?
options: Its nodes are points of interest, and every pair of points is directly connected
Its nodes are points of interest, and directly connected edges are weighted by natural walking time
Its nodes are matched zones, and directly connected edges are weighted by Euclidean distance
Its nodes are points of interest, and directly connected edges are weighted by Euclidean distance
questions.explanation: In the minimum-time approach, the graph's nodes are points of interest, directly connected edges use Euclidean distance as weights, and the graph need not be complete.

questions.question: Why are travel times computed for pairs of vertices in the minimum-time approach?
options: To compute a new cybersickness threshold for each vertex
To form a complete graph whose weights remain Euclidean distances
To form a complete, time-weighted graph that can be given to a TSP solver
To avoid introducing hypothetical edges between unconnected vertices
questions.explanation: Travel times computed with the natural walking speed model become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and that complete graph is supplied to a TSP solver.

questions.question: What must be done to the optimal path returned by a TSP solver before it becomes the final solution path?
options: Any directly connected edges in the path must be removed
Any Euclidean-distance edges in the path must be removed
Any hypothetical nodes in the path must be removed
Any hypothetical edges in the path must be removed
questions.explanation: The TSP solver's optimal path may contain hypothetical edges, and those edges must be removed before the final solution path is produced.

items.reason: Speed, teleport, and terrain can be used to reduce exposure duration, while the natural walking model is described as a presence-enhancing model rather than an experience-optimization method.

questions.question: Why can a realistic natural walking model be used in a cybersickness-aware VR tour optimizer even though the model itself is not an optimization technique?
questions.reference_answer: The natural walking model creates a realistic sense of movement by displaying optic flow that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, and its direct role is to enhance presence rather than optimize the experience. It can still be used in cybersickness-aware optimization because cybersickness is correlated with VR exposure duration, and shorter exposure can reduce or minimize symptom onset. Therefore, the optimizer can keep the tour realistic while the path-planning task limits the exposure duration that contributes to cybersickness.

questions.question: Why does a VR travel-time optimization algorithm convert an incomplete virtual-world graph into a complete time-weighted graph before using a standard TSP solver?
questions.reference_answer: The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph whose vertices are points of interest and whose directly connected edges are weighted by Euclidean distance, but the graph need not be complete because not every point of interest has a direct path to another. Standard TSP is posed on a complete graph, so the algorithm adds hypothetical edges with shortest-path lengths and then produces a complete time-weighted graph by replacing edge weights with travel times computed by the natural walking speed model. A standard TSP solver can then find the optimal time and path, and any hypothetical edge in that path is replaced by the corresponding shortest path in the original graph.

questions.question: Why might a minimum-time path that covers all points of interest still be insufficient for reducing cybersickness, and how does a time-limited path approach address that limitation?
questions.reference_answer: The minimum-time approach searches for a route that covers all points of interest in the least possible time, but if the virtual environment is large, that optimal time can still exceed the cybersickness time threshold. The alternative approach therefore uses a fixed time limit and searches for a route that covers the maximum possible number of points of interest within that limit. This is useful because cybersickness increases with exposure duration, so bounding the total tour time bounds the exposure that can cause symptoms.
